The Nicotine Acetylcholine Receptor is the cell receptor that the virus binds to in order to enter cells. The virus enters the cell by way of a process called endocytosis, specifically pinocytosis. Once inside the cell, the virus uses the acidic environment of the endosome to bind to the endosome's membrane and release its five proteins (N, P, M, G, and L) and single-strand RNA into the cytoplasm.

Within a muscle or nerve cell, the virus undergoes replication. The L protein transcribes five mRNA strands and a positive strand of RNA from the original negative strand RNA using free nucleotides in the cytoplasm. These five mRNA strands are then translated into their corresponding proteins (P, L, N, G, and M proteins) at free ribosomes in the cytoplasm. Some proteins require post-translational modifications, such as the G protein, which travels through the rough endoplasmic reticulum, undergoes further folding, and is then transported to the Golgi apparatus, where a sugar group is added to it (glycosylation).

When there are enough viral proteins, the viral polymerase will begin to synthesize new negative strands of RNA from the template of the positive strand RNA. The new negative strands will then be used to produce more viral mRNA and proteins, allowing the virus to replicate and spread throughout the cell.

These are two islands, separated by a very narrow strait; they are ten thousand furlongs distant from Africa, and are called the Islands of the Blessed. They enjoy moderate rains at long intervals, and winds which for the most part are soft and precipitate dews, so that the islands not only have a rich soil which is excellent for plowing and planting, but also produce a natural fruit that is plentiful and wholesome enough to feed, without toil or trouble, a leisured folk. Moreover, an air that is salubrious, owing to the climate and the moderate changes in the seasons, prevails on the islands. For the north and east winds which blow out from our part of the world plunge into fathomless space, and, owing to the distance, dissipate themselves and lose their power before they reach the islands; while the south and west winds that envelope the islands sometimes bring in their train soft and intermittent showers, but for the most part cool them with moist breezes and gently nourish the soil. Therefore a firm belief has made its way, even to the Barbarians, that here is the Elysian Field and the abode of the blessed.

lm_output: The acetylcholine receptor is the most likely cell receptor that the virus interacts with to enter cells. The virus enters the cell by way of endocytosis, specifically pinocytosis. Once inside the cell, the virus uses the acidic environment of the endosome to bind to its membrane, releasing its five proteins (N, P, M, G, and L) and single-strand RNA into the cytoplasm. Within a muscle or nerve cell, the virus undergoes replication. The L protein transcribes five mRNA strands and a positive strand of RNA from the original negative strand RNA using free nucleotides in the cytoplasm. These five mRNA strands are then translated into their corresponding proteins (P, L, N, G, and M proteins) at free ribosomes in the cytoplasm. Some proteins require post-translational modifications, such as the glycoprotein (G protein), which travels through the rough endoplasmic reticulum, undergoes further folding, and is then transported to the Golgi apparatus, where a sugar group is added to it (glycosylation). When there are enough viral proteins, the viral polymerase will begin to synthesize new negative strands of RNA from the template of the positive strand RNA. This process allows the virus to replicate and infect more cells.

The acetylcholine receptor is the most likely cell receptor that the virus interacts with to enter cells. The virus enters the cell by way of endocytosis, specifically pinocytosis. Once inside the cell, the virus uses the acidic environment of the endosome to bind to its membrane and release its five proteins (N, P, M, G, and L) and single-strand RNA into the cytoplasm.

Within a muscle or nerve cell, the virus undergoes replication. The L protein transcribes five mRNA strands and a positive strand of RNA from the original negative strand RNA using free nucleotides in the cytoplasm. These five mRNA strands are then translated into their corresponding proteins (P, L, N, G, and M proteins) at free ribosomes in the cytoplasm. Some proteins require post-translational modifications, such as the glycoprotein (G protein) which travels through the rough endoplasmic reticulum, undergoes further folding, and is then transported to the Golgi apparatus where a sugar group is added to it (glycosylation).

When there are enough viral proteins, the viral polymerase will begin to synthesize new negative strands of RNA from the template of the positive strand RNA. These new negative strands will then be used as templates to produce more mRNA strands, which will be translated into more viral proteins, and the cycle will continue, allowing the virus to replicate and spread.

This was a direct reference by Marx to Hegel's Elements of the Philosophy of Right §63 as Marx adds: A thing can be a use value, without having value. This is the case whenever its utility to man is not due to labour. Such are air, virgin soil, natural meadows, &c. A thing can be useful, and the product of human labour, without being a commodity. Whoever directly satisfies his wants with the produce of his own labour, creates, indeed, use values, but not commodities. In order to produce the latter, he must not only produce use values, but use values for others, social use values. (And not only for others, without more. The mediaeval peasant produced quit-rent-corn for his feudal lord and tithe-corn for his parson. But neither the quit-rent-corn nor the tithe-corn became commodities by reason of the fact that they had been produced for others.
